parole.significato: A leading away; a carrying away.
parole.testo: From Latin abductiō(n) (“a robbing; an abduction”), from abdūcō (“to take or lead away”), from ab (“away”) + dūcō (“to lead”). By surface analysis, abduct + -ion or abduce + -tion. * (physiology): From French, from Latin abductus. * Compare French abduction.

parole.significato: of albumin
parole.testo: From albumin (from Latin albumen (“egg white”) via French albumine) + -oid. Ultimately from Latin albus (“white”).

parole.significato: The plea or mode of defense under which a person on trial for a crime proves or attempts to prove being in another plac…
parole.testo: From the 18th century, from Latin alibī (“elsewhere, at another place”, adverb). Probably after French alibi, which has this use since the late 14th century.

parole.significato: Pertaining to, or having the form of, a ring: in the shape of an annulus.
parole.testo: From Latin ānulāris (“ring-shaped”); (possibly through French annulaire), from ānulus (“ring”).

parole.significato: Desirable; capable or worthy of being the object of desire.
parole.testo: From Latin appetibilis, from appetere: compare French appétible.

parole.significato: Synonym of art for art's sake.
parole.testo: Latin translation of French l'art pour l'art. See the main entry for more.

parole.significato: Synonym of astroite.
parole.testo: Latin astroites: compare French astroite.

parole.significato: Synonym of astroite.
parole.testo: Latin astroites: compare French astroite.

parole.significato: A radiated fossil or stone; a starstone.
parole.testo: Latin astroites: compare French astroite.

parole.significato: Anything whatsoever, as a ruling, by the judge of a lower court in a matter pending an appeal.
parole.testo: A variant of attemptate assimilated to Latin attentātus and French attentat.

parole.significato: Of good omen; indicating future success.
parole.testo: From auspice + -ious, from Latin auspicium (“augury”), from auspex (“augur”), possibly via French.

parole.significato: A plant, the Impatiens balsamina, or garden balsam.
parole.testo: From Latin balsamina (“balsam plant”) (perhaps via French balsamine), from Ancient Greek βαλσαμίνη (balsamínē). The Latin name of the unrelated balsam plant must have been applied to Impatiens balsamina soon after it arrived in Europe- Leonhart Fuchs referred to it as balsamina as early as 1542.

parole.significato: One who benefits or receives an advantage.
parole.testo: From Latin beneficiarius (“enjoying a favor, granted a privilege”) from beneficium (“benefit”), perhaps via or influenced by French bénéficiaire (“beneficiary”). Indirectly, by way of the etymology of the Latin word beneficium, the English word beneficiary ultimately has the same origin as the Engli

parole.significato: A brevipennate (short-winged) bird, in a former proposed classification, Brevipennes
parole.testo: From Latin brevis (“short”) + penna (“wing”). Compare French brévipenne.

parole.significato: Shoe-shaped, shaped like a shoe.
parole.testo: From Latin calceus (“calceus, footwear”) + English -form (“-shaped”) after the model of French calcéiforme.

parole.significato: Synonym of celestial.
parole.testo: From Latin caelestis (“heavenly”), probably via French céleste, from caelum (“sky, heavens, Heaven”).

parole.significato: A group of 1000 things, particularly
parole.testo: From Latin chilias (“the number 1000, a group of 1000 things”), possibly via French chiliade, from Ancient Greek χιλιάς (khiliás, “the number 1000, any large amount, a millennium”), from χῑ́λιοι (khī́lioi, “1000”) + -ᾰ́ς (-ắs, “-ad: forming collective nouns”). Equivalent to chilia- + -ad.

parole.significato: Synonym of millenarian: a person who believes the Second Coming of Jesus Christ will involve his physical rule on Earth…
parole.testo: From Latin chiliasta, possibly via French chiliaste, from Ancient Greek χιλιαστής (khiliastḗs), from χῑ́λιοι (khī́lioi, “thousand”) + -αστής (-astḗs, “-ast, -ist: forming agent nouns”). Equivalent to chilia- + -ast.

parole.significato: incineration; reduction to ashes
parole.testo: From Latin cinefactio, from cinis (“ashes”) + facere (“to make”). Compare French cinéfaction.

parole.significato: Having, feeling or showing compassion (to or toward someone).
parole.testo: Pseudo-Latinism, derived from a pseudo-Latin form of French compassionné, past participle of compassionner (“to feel sorry for”). By surface analysis, compassion + -ate.

parole.significato: Rule by consuls, as during most periods of the Roman Republic or in France between 1799 and 1804.
parole.testo: From Middle English consulat, consulate, from Latin consulātus, from consul + -ātus. In some senses, via French consulat. By surface analysis, consul + -ate (forms nouns denoting rank or office).

parole.significato: The act of adorning, embellishing, or honoring; ornamentation.
parole.testo: From Latin decoratio: compare French décoration. Morphologically decorate + -ion.

parole.significato: Act of tasting; a slight trial.
parole.testo: Latin delibatio: compare French délibation.

parole.significato: The coexistence in a given population of two closely related native languages or dialects, one of which is regarded as…
parole.testo: From Latin diglōssia. In linguistics introduced 1959 by Charles A. Ferguson, based on French diglossie, from Ancient Greek δίγλωσσος (díglōssos, “bilingual”) + -ία (-ía). Equivalent to di- + -glossia.

parole.significato: Eloquent.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin disertus or French disert.

parole.significato: Someone who writes or performs a dissertation or speech.
parole.testo: Latin: compare French dissertateur.

parole.significato: Pertaining to an enigma.
parole.testo: From Latin aenigmaticus and French énigmatique, from Ancient Greek αἰνιγματικός (ainigmatikós); equivalent to enigma + -tic.

parole.significato: Of or containing iron.
parole.testo: From ferro- + -ous, from Latin ferreus directly or via French ferreux, from ferrum (“iron”) + -eus (“-ous: forming adjectives”).

parole.significato: The act of bending a joint, especially a bone joint; the counteraction of extension.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin flexiō, from flectō (“to bend, curve”) + -tiō, possibly via French. By surface analysis, flex + -ion.

parole.significato: Making void; rendering null.
parole.testo: Latin frustrotorius: compare French frustratoire.

parole.significato: A unit of measure used in the 16th century, defined as "five feet" or "five geometrical feet".
parole.testo: Calque of Latin passus geometricus or French pas géometrique.

parole.significato: A stage actor.
parole.testo: From Latin histriō. Compare French histrion. See histrionic.

parole.significato: moistening.
parole.testo: Latin humectatio: compare French humectation.

parole.significato: The act of swallowing greedily or immoderately; gulp.
parole.testo: Latin ingurgitatio: compare French ingurgitation.

parole.significato: inward; internal; intimate
parole.testo: From Latin intimus (“innermost”) perhaps via French intime. Compare intimate (adjective).

parole.significato: Lying stretched out.
parole.testo: From Latin jacens, present participle of jacere (“to lie”): compare French jacent. Doublet of jessant.

parole.significato: Darting, shooting or throwing out suddenly
parole.testo: Latin jaculatorius: compare French jaculatoire.

parole.significato: A chained iron collar once used in churches to expose sinners to public scorn.
parole.testo: From Latin iugum (“yoke”), possibly via French jougs.

parole.significato: One who justifies or vindicates.
parole.testo: Latin; compare French justificateur

parole.significato: To assuage or mitigate; to soften (fever/pain/effects etc.).
parole.testo: From Latin lēnis (“soft, mild”) + -ify. Compare French lénifier. See lenition.

parole.significato: A phrase or expression peculiar to or characteristic of a given person or group of people.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin locūtiō, locūtiōnem (“speech”), from loquor (“speak”). Compare the French cognate locution.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to (ritual) purification.
parole.testo: From Latin lūstrālis, from lūstrum (“purificatory sacrifice”); compare French lustral. See lustrum.

parole.significato: An official or authoritative command; an order or injunction; a commission; a judicial precept; an authorization.
parole.testo: First attested in 1521; borrowed from Latin mandātum (“a charge, order, command, commission, injunction”), substantivized from the neuter forms of mandātus, perfect passive participle of mandō (“to commit to one's charge, order, command, commission, literally to put into one's hands”) (see -ate (nou

parole.significato: Characterized by very precise, conscientious attention to details.
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin meticulōsus (“full of fear, timid, fearful, terrible, frightful”), from metus (“fear”) and -culōsus, extracted from perīculōsus (“perilous”). Sense of “characterized by very precise, conscientious attention to details” is a semantic loan from French méticuleux.

parole.significato: Materials of war: armaments, weapons and ammunition.
parole.testo: From Latin mūnitiō (“a defence, fortification”) via French munition, from mūnīre (“fortify, defend (with a wall)”) + -tiō, from moenia (“city walls, defensive walls, or walls in general”). Equivalent to munite + -ion.

parole.significato: A follower of Novatianism.
parole.testo: From Latin Novatius (plausibly via French Novatien).

parole.significato: Of or relating to lice.
parole.testo: From Latin pedicularis, from pediculus (“louse”). Compare French pédiculaire. By surface analysis, pedic(u)le + -ar.

parole.significato: Money paid at fairs for permission to set up booths.
parole.testo: Latin piccadium, from French piquer (“to prick”).

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, resembling, or containing lead.
parole.testo: From Latin plumbum (“lead”) + -ic, originally in calques of French plombique, from plomb (“lead”) + -ique (“-ic”). See also molybdic.

parole.significato: Of momentous or ominous significance.
parole.testo: Of multiple origins: * Borrowed from Latin portentōsus, from portentus (“predicted”) + -ōsus. Compare earlier portentuous (via Middle English from Latin portentuōsus). By surface analysis, portent + -ous. * Borrowed from French portentueux

parole.significato: derived from Prussian blue
parole.testo: From Latin prussicus (“Prussian”) or French prussique.

parole.significato: An alto ophicleide.
parole.testo: From Latin quīnque (“five”) + clavis (“key”), formed as a calque of French quinte à clef.

parole.significato: Synonym of roborant: strengthening, invigorating, or restorative.
parole.testo: From Latin rōborāre (“to strengthen, to invigorate”) + -ive (“forming adjectives”) directly and via French roboratif, from rōbur (“reddish oak; hardness, strength”) + -āre (“forming verbs”). Equivalent to roborate + -ive.

parole.significato: The act of sowing or spreading.
parole.testo: Latin seminatio: compare French sémination.

parole.significato: Pertaining to mirrors; mirror-like, reflective.
parole.testo: From Latin speculāris, from speculum; and in some senses from speculārī (“to watch, observe”). Some later senses via French spéculaire.

parole.significato: To produce or emit sperm.
parole.testo: From Latin spermatizare (“to spermatize”), possibly via French spermatiser, from Ancient Greek σπερματίζειν (spermatízein, “to sow, spread seed upon”), from σπέρμα (spérma, “seed, sperm”). By surface analysis, spermat- + -ize.

parole.significato: A livid mark; a blow; a bruise.
parole.testo: From Latin suggillatio, ultimately from suggillo. Compare French suggillation.

parole.significato: The state or quality of being sumptuous; wealth; high price
parole.testo: From sumptuo(u)s + -ity, from Latin sumptuositas: compare French somptuosité.

parole.significato: A person or thing that translates meaning from one language into another, particularly
parole.testo: Directly from Latin trānslātor and French translator, and also from Middle English translatour, from Old French translatour, translateur, etc., from Latin trānslātor, from trānslātus (“carried across”) + -or (“-er: forming agent nouns”), from trānsferō (“carry across”), from trans (“across”) + ferō

parole.significato: Synonym of interpreter.
parole.testo: From mediaeval Latin turchemannus or French trucheman, from Arabic تُرْجُمَان (turjumān). Doublet of dragoman.

parole.significato: Pertaining to ulmin; designating an acid obtained from ulmin.
parole.testo: Formed from the root of Latin ulmus (“an elm”), with the suffix -ic: compare French ulmique.

parole.significato: highly censurable; worthy of vituperation or severe censure.
parole.testo: From Latin vĭtŭpĕrābĭlis: compare French vitupérable.
